storm.summary_layperson: A weak, nearly stationary cluster of showers sits about 30 miles west of the cove and isn't closing in on the 5–10 PM window, though NWS is watching for a better chance of thunderstorms and heavy rain arriving overnight as a warm front moves through.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound's marine layer is present but weak — a 5.6°F water–air gap, short of the roughly 10°F needed to reliably choke storms here.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows a single modest cell about 32 miles west of the cove, topping out at 38 dBZ — real precipitation, not clutter, but on the weak side. Instability is low: CAPE sits at just 530 J/kg, well under the ~1500 J/kg mark that supports vigorous storms. Deep-layer shear is a more respectable 27 kt from the SW, which is in the gray zone (20–35 kt) where outcome depends on how organized the cell is — but with CAPE this low, there isn't much fuel for shear to organize in the first place.

The Sound's stabilizing effect is only partly in play today. Water is 75°F against 80–81°F air, a 5.6°F delta — enough for a weak marine layer, but below the roughly 10°F gap this pipeline treats as the threshold for a reliably protective mechanism, so protective_mechanism_active reads false. Call the local effect neutral rather than protective: there's some choking potential given the low CAPE, but not enough of a stable layer to count on it.

Radar-tracked motion for this cell failed (the frame-to-frame centroid implied an unphysical 184 kt, discarded as a growth/decay artifact), so the arrival engine fell back to modeled HRRR steering. Even so, the cell's projected closing speed toward the cove is only about 1 kt — it's essentially parked to the west, not meaningfully approaching, so there's no useful ETA to quote for this window. No NWS alerts are active.

The bigger story sits just past this window's edge: the OKX Area Forecast Discussion flags a warm front moving in this evening with deepening moisture, and explicitly calls out potential for training thunderstorms and rainfall rates over 1 in/hr late tonight into Monday — well after 10 PM. The extended HRRR outlook (hours 7–12 past this cycle, i.e. overnight) shows CAPE climbing toward a mean of ~1170 J/kg, still moderate but notably higher than right now. What would change tonight's call for the 5–10 PM window specifically: the parked cell actually starting to move toward the cove, or CAPE building faster than modeled.

wind.tactics_blurb: Sea breeze reinforced by a light onshore gradient — a steady S breeze around 10–11 kt holds through sunset (8:09 PM), then eases and backs toward SSE as the thermal shuts off. Pressure is fairly even across the cove early; favor the west side as it softens and backs late.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a sea-breeze day reinforced by the background gradient (A+): the air–water temperature gap (deltaT) is 5.6°F — enough to clear the ~5°F thermal threshold — and the gradient wind is onshore (S/SE, ~9.7 kt average across the well-sited stations) rather than fighting it, so it's adding to the sea breeze instead of opposing it. Sea-breeze coverage across the coastal station network is at 65% southerly with 0% inland, which lands in the “moderate and building” range — real, but not the fully mature, all-stations-flipped version of the pattern.

HRRR's own hourly forecast is lagging reality: the model has the surface wind at SE (~130°) through the window, but Riverside YC and the western-Sound station cluster are already reading S (177°) — a 48° divergence. Because deltaT is under the 8°F gate this pipeline uses for a full model correction, no formal veer adjustment was applied, so the table above leans on the observed direction as the anchor for the early hours rather than the raw HRRR guess.

Pressure across the course should be fairly uniform in S–SSE flow, per the cove's geography — no single side gets a big edge while the breeze holds S. As the evening wears on past the 8:09 PM sunset and the wind eases and backs toward SSE, expect Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) to start sheltering the east shore, tipping the advantage toward the west side (Belle Haven/Field Point) for the last hour or two of the window.

Shift character: with the sea breeze only moderately developed (not the fully-flipped, all-subregion version), expect modest oscillations (±10° or so) around a S mean rather than large swings, persistent rather than wildly shifty. After sunset there's no thermal to sustain the pattern, so direction will drift rather than oscillate cleanly.

Fleet impact: 10–11 kt through the front half of the window is squarely in the one-design dinghy sweet spot — good, straightforward racing. By 9–10 PM, as the thermal fades and speed drops toward 6–7 kt, it edges into light-air/drifter territory — still sailable, just softer and more finicky on the shifts.

data_caveats: Buoy 44040 / WLIS readings are 75–87 min old — the over-water sea-breeze depth signal may lag current conditions somewhat.

Radar-based storm motion tracking failed this cycle (centroid displacement implied an unphysical 184 kt); the arrival engine fell back to modeled HRRR steering, and the tracked cell is only creeping toward the cove (~1 kt closing) with no reliable ETA to quote.
